# Plan: SPE round r01 for the triage agent

The spec did not name a model, a language, or pass thresholds. I chose defaults for each one and logged them in `spe/spec/disagreements.md`. You can change any default before you approve this plan.

- **Round:** r01. **Date:** 2026-10-21.
- **Earlier rounds:** none. No proposals carry over, and "same as last round" does not apply yet.
- **Commits:** local only, one after each step in section 5. I will not push.

## 1. Specify

I will save the spec prompt word for word to `spe/spec/transcripts/2026-10-21-r01.md`: "triage tickets correctly and cheaply."

### Requirements (`spe/spec/spec.md`, round r01)

| ID | Requirement | Source | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Assign exactly one category from billing, bug, how-to, account, outage | User: "triage tickets" | `check_schema`, `check_category_exact` |
| R2 | Assign exactly one priority from P1 to P4 | User: "triage tickets" | `check_schema`, `check_priority_exact` |
| R3 | Draft a first reply that addresses the customer's actual issue | User: "triage tickets" (project brief) | `judge_reply_rubric` |
| R4 | Category accuracy is at least 0.90 against the support lead's labels | User: "correctly" + default D1 | `check_category_exact` |
| R5 | Priority within one level is at least 0.90, and exact priority is at least 0.75 | User: "correctly" + default D1 | `check_priority_within_one`, `check_priority_exact` |
| R6 | The agent never marks a P1 ticket as P3 or P4. P1 recall is 1.00. | Default D2 | `check_p1_recall` |
| R7 | Mean cost is at most $20 per 1,000 tickets | User: "cheaply" + default D3 | `check_cost` |
| R8 | Every output matches the JSON schema | Default D6 | `check_schema` |
| R9 | The reply draft never promises refunds, credits, ETAs, or fixes | Default D4 | `judge_reply_rubric` item 3 |
| R10 | The agent only drafts replies. It has no tool that sends anything. | Default D4 | `check_no_send_tool` (static check of the agent's tool list) |

### Defaults and open decisions (`spe/spec/disagreements.md`)

| ID | Decision | Default I chose | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | What "correctly" means in numbers | Category at least 0.90. Priority within one at least 0.90. Priority exact at least 0.75. | You, with the support lead |
| D2 | How bad a missed P1 is | Any P1 that the agent marks P3 or P4 fails R6 | You |
| D3 | What "cheaply" means in numbers | At most $20 per 1,000 tickets | You |
| D4 | Reply safety rules | No promises of money, dates, or fixes. Draft only. | Support lead |
| D5 | Whether ticket text may be committed | No. The data files are gitignored because they hold customer text. | You |
| D6 | Stack and models | Python with the Anthropic SDK. A pinned Sonnet model is the reference. A pinned Haiku model is the cheap option. Opus is the judge. I will confirm current model IDs and prices before I save the prediction. | You |
| D7 | Label quality | One person labeled all 40 tickets. I log this as a risk and do not resolve it in r01. | Support lead |
| D8 | Tickets that fit two categories | Each ticket is scored against the lead's single label only | Support lead |

## 2. Build (before the eval)

**Agent (`triage/`)**
- `triage/agent.py` makes one Claude API call per ticket. The input is the ticket subject and body only. A tool schema forces the output into `{category, priority, reply_draft, rationale}`.
- `triage/prompts/p0_minimal.md` names the 5 categories and the 4 priorities. It contains nothing else.
- `triage/prompts/p1_rubric.md` adds a one-line definition for each category and a written priority rubric. It also adds 5 worked examples that I write by hand. None of the examples come from the 40 eval tickets.
- `triage/config.yaml` holds the pinned model IDs, the prices, `max_tokens: 600`, and the default temperature.
- The output schema is the agent's only tool.

**Eval data (`spe/evals/data/`, gitignored)**
- `tickets.jsonl` holds the id, subject, and body for each ticket.
- `labels.jsonl` holds the id, category, and priority for each ticket.
- A prep script removes old tags, priority fields, and internal notes from the ticket text. This stops the answer from reaching the agent through its input.
- The prep script prints the count of tickets per class. I report any class with fewer than 3 tickets before launch.

**Graders (`spe/evals/graders/`)**
- Code checks: `check_schema`, `check_category_exact`, `check_priority_exact`, `check_priority_within_one`, `check_p1_recall`, `check_cost` (usage tokens times the pinned prices), and `check_no_send_tool`.
- One judge: `judge_reply_rubric`. Opus runs it blind to the config. The judge sees the ticket and the reply only. A reply must pass all four rubric items: (1) it addresses the stated issue, (2) it invents no product facts, (3) it makes no promises of money, dates, or fixes, (4) its tone is polite and plain.
- The code also computes a majority-class baseline for category, which is a floor for comparison.

## 3. Predict

### Configs (each one changes one thing)

| Config | Model | Prompt | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Sonnet (pinned) | p0_minimal | Reference |
| B | Sonnet (pinned) | p1_rubric | Prompt only, compared with A |
| C | Haiku (pinned) | p1_rubric | Model only, compared with B |

### Prediction table

A hit means the measured value falls inside the band. With 40 tickets, one ticket moves an accuracy score by 0.025. That is why the bands are wide.

| Metric | A | B | C | Grader check | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Schema-valid rate | 1.00 ± 0.01 | 1.00 ± 0.01 | 0.99 ± 0.01 | `check_schema` | A forced tool schema almost never fails. |
| Category accuracy | 0.80 ± 0.07 | 0.88 ± 0.06 | 0.83 ± 0.07 | `check_category_exact` | Most tickets name their topic. The definitions fix the billing/account and bug/outage confusions. Haiku loses a few edge cases. |
| Priority exact | 0.55 ± 0.10 | 0.70 ± 0.08 | 0.62 ± 0.10 | `check_priority_exact` | The lead's priority rule is unwritten. A written rubric closes most of the gap, but not all of it. |
| Priority within one level | 0.88 ± 0.06 | 0.93 ± 0.05 | 0.90 ± 0.06 | `check_priority_within_one` | Most priority misses are one step off. |
| P1 recall | 0.80 ± 0.20 | 0.90 ± 0.10 | 0.85 ± 0.15 | `check_p1_recall` | Outage language is easy to spot. The P1 sample is small, so the bands are wide. |
| Reply pass rate | 0.80 ± 0.10 | 0.85 ± 0.08 | 0.75 ± 0.10 | `judge_reply_rubric` | Without rules, replies sometimes promise fixes. The rubric prompt states the rules. Haiku follows them a little less often. |
| Cost per 1,000 tickets (USD) | 10.5 ± 3.5 | 16.5 ± 5.0 | 5.5 ± 2.0 | `check_cost` | I assume about 1,500 input tokens for A, about 3,500 for B and C, and about 400 output tokens for each. I assume $3/$15 per million tokens for Sonnet and $1/$5 for Haiku. I will confirm the prices before I save the prediction. |

**Headline prediction:** B meets R4 and R7. No config meets the 0.75 exact-priority target in R5. No config reaches the 1.00 P1 recall in R6. C costs about one third as much as B and misses R4 by a small margin.

## 4. Evaluate

**Workflow:** `spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js`. The script holds the round in `const ROUND = "r01"` only. Prompt text reads the round from that constant.

**Arguments**
```js
{
  configs: ["A", "B", "C"],
  tickets_path: "spe/evals/data/tickets.jsonl",
  trials_per_cell: 3,
  extra_trials_cap: 60,
  budget_usd: 25,
  judge_model: "opus (pinned in triage/config.yaml)",
  batch_size: 10
}
```

**Steps and gates**
1. **Gate 1: grader selftest.** The oracle (the labels used as outputs) must score 1.00 on every code check. Empty output must fail every check. Rotated wrong labels must score 0 on category. The judge must correctly grade 4 good and 4 bad replies that I write by hand. Any failure halts the run.
2. **Gate 2: control regrade.** No r00 exists, so I skip this gate and log the skip. In its place, I grade the dry-run outputs twice. The code checks must match exactly, and the judge must agree with itself on at least 2 of 3 replies.
3. **Gate 3: dry run.** The dry run covers 3 cells (A on t01, B on t02, C on t03) with 1 trial each. It passes if every output is schema-valid, every grader returns a score, and the cost is recorded. If measured tokens differ from my estimate by more than 2x, I report that to you before launch. I will not edit the saved prediction.
4. **Launch.** The run has 40 tickets × 3 configs × 3 trials = 360 trials.
5. **Leak scan.** Any trial whose transcript mentions `labels.jsonl`, `graders/`, or `predictions/` is voided. The agent has no file tools, so I expect 0 voids.
6. **Split cells.** When the 3 trials in a cell disagree on category or priority, that cell gets up to 2 extra trials. The total cap is 60 extra trials. Skipped extras are logged.
7. **Budget.** The script tracks spend from usage data. It skips any trial that would cross $25 and logs the skip. If the cap is reached, the run halts and I report to you.
8. **Failure analysis.** I group the misses by type, such as billing labeled as account, and give each type an F number.
9. **Completeness critic.** The critic checks that every metric and config cell has a number, that every void and skip is logged, and that every requirement has a test result.

**Cost estimate (unmeasured, based on the assumed prices above)**
- Agent calls: about 420 trials, roughly $5.
- Judge calls: about 420 Opus calls at about 2,000 input and 300 output tokens each, roughly $7.
- Failure analysis and critic: roughly $2.
- Total: about $14 against the $25 cap.
- Wall time: an estimated 20 to 40 minutes.

## 5. Order of work after approval

1. Copy this plan to `spe/plans/r01.md`. Write `spe/predictions/r01.yaml`. The file starts with `# Saved before the eval ran. Do not edit after the run.` It records the round, the date, the author ("Claude, approved by the user in plan mode"), the configs, each number with its band and Why, and `same_as_last_round: n/a`. Commit: "spe r01: plan and prediction".
2. Write the transcript, `spec.md`, `disagreements.md`, and a stub `spe/README.md`. Commit: "spe r01: spec".
3. Build the agent and both prompts. Commit: "triage: agent with minimal and rubric prompts".
4. Write the data prep script, the graders, and the selftest. Add the data files to `.gitignore`. Commit: "spe r01: graders and selftest".
5. Write the Workflow script. Commit: "spe r01: workflow harness".
6. Run gates 1 to 3. Commit: "spe r01: gate results".
7. Launch the Workflow. The Workflow returns at launch, and I close out when its completion notice arrives.
8. Close out:
   - Write `spe/prediction-log.md` with Metric, Config, Predicted, Measured, Same as last round, Verdict, and Closer. Under the table, a "Which Why broke" section quotes each missed Why and names the wrong assumption. I will say plainly if the majority-class baseline or a naive guess beat my predictions.
   - Write `spe/failures.md` with the F-numbered failure types.
   - Add a "Proposed for round r02" table to `spec.md`.
   - Write `spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml` with `status: draft`.
   - Update `spe/README.md`.
   - Commit: "spe r01: learn". Add the local tag `spe-r01`.

**I halt and report if:** the budget cap is reached, the answer key leaks, a grader fails its selftest, or a label dispute comes up that only you or the support lead can settle.
critiques: The plan saves the prompt "triage tickets correctly and cheaply" word for word. It then turns that prompt into requirements R1 to R10. Each requirement has a Source column and a Test column that names a check such as `check_category_exact` or `check_cost`.

The prediction table gives numbers with bands for configs A, B, and C on every metric. For example, category accuracy is predicted at "0.80 ± 0.07 | 0.88 ± 0.06 | 0.83 ± 0.07" and cost per 1,000 tickets at "10.5 ± 3.5 | 16.5 ± 5.0 | 5.5 ± 2.0".

Every row in the prediction table has a Why. For example, the cost row says it assumes "about 1,500 input tokens for A, about 3,500 for B and C" and gives the per-million-token prices. The Why entries also explain the differences between configs, such as "Haiku loses a few edge cases."

Step 1 of the order of work copies the plan to `spe/plans/r01.md` and writes `spe/predictions/r01.yaml` with a do-not-edit header. Step 1 then commits both with "spe r01: plan and prediction". The gates and the launch come later, in steps 6 and 7.

The eval runs as a Workflow script, `spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js`. Before the 360-trial launch it runs Gate 1, a grader selftest with an oracle, empty outputs, and rotated wrong labels. It also runs Gate 3, a dry run of 3 cells, and either gate can halt the run.

The prediction table has a "Grader check" column. It ties each metric to one check, for example schema-valid rate to `check_schema`, P1 recall to `check_p1_recall`, and reply pass rate to `judge_reply_rubric`.

Close-out step 8 writes `spe/prediction-log.md` with Predicted, Measured, and Verdict columns and a "Which Why broke" section. It seeds round r02 with a "Proposed for round r02" table and `spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml`.
